item.title: Out of Deathknell
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The spider that killed him did not pause to consider the Light. Night Web’s Hollow is an old gold mine northwest of Deathknell. The Forsaken want the gold still in it; the Night Web Spiders want what walks in after it. One of them got to Ghoulsbie first.
item.content:encoded:
The spider that killed him did not pause to consider the Light. Night Web’s Hollow is an old gold mine northwest of Deathknell. The Forsaken want the gold still in it; the Night Web Spiders want what walks in after it. One of them got to Ghoulsbie first.

His corpse lay on the webbing and wet stone with the same grey-green face the grave had given him, dark hair matted, yellow eyes still open. His spirit stood over the body the way a disappointed officer stands over a recruit. Ghoulsbie looked irritated to be charged twice.

He had earned the visit. Before the mine he finished Scavenging Deathknell for Deathguard Saltain, picking through boxes so the next corpses out of the ground will not walk away naked, and Rattling the Rattlecages for Shadow Priest Sarvis until the Lich King’s leftover skeletons were thin enough to satisfy him. He finished Rediscovering the Light as well — the Injured Deathguards he had left waiting last time — and the heal still burned going out of him. Aramis Hammerhand had said it would.

He had already granted Marla’s Last Wish on the way. Samuel Fipps, who murdered his own wife after the plague took his mind, is buried now beside her in the first row of the chapel graveyard. Novice Elreth hoped they would find peace together. In Tirisfal that is a great deal to hope.

Executor Arren needed the spiders cleared so someone could take gold out of that hole. Aramis needed something kinder. A Light in the Darkness: the freshly raised fools wrapped in silk along the tunnel walls were the proof that not even death can stop the Light. He cut them out of their cocoons and thinned the spiders enough for Arren to call it a start. Then one of the ones still left in the dark made a better argument than his blade did.

He rose again, because that is the joke of his kind, and went west of the chapel into the hills. Coming to Terms: not every paladin who climbs out of the dirt can bear being the thing they once hunted. The Frightened Paladin wanted no hand and no sermon. She chose a clean end over Forsaken life, and Ghoulsbie granted it. Aramis said he would say a prayer to the Light for her.

The Scarlets came next, because they always do. Arren’s scouts had found a camp southeast of Deathknell — Converts and Initiates who will not rest until every undead, Scourge or no, is ash. Ghoulsbie took their armbands up the ridgeline under those sickly shafts of light Tirisfal calls a sun.

Then he took their messenger. Meven Korgal had come down from the Scarlet Monastery with papers Arren wanted more than another corpse. The Red Messenger died in front of his tent, and among the boasts and scouting reports Arren found a map of their field commanders.

Vital Intelligence sent him north out of Deathknell, east at the fork, past Cold Hearth Manor — once known for warmth and harvest, known now for neither. Calvin Montague pressed a nondescript letter on him for Innkeeper Renee. Deathguard Simmer sent him west to Solliden Farmstead to steal ten pumpkins from the living humans who still farm there under Scarlet protection. He took the pumpkins, crossed Nightmare Vale, and accepted Gordo’s gloom-weed errand without slowing down.

Brill received him the way Brill receives everyone: with more work. Executor Zygand took the Scarlet documents and immediately handed him a war: At War With The Scarlet Crusade, a wanted notice for Maggot Eye, and two quieter tasks named Discipline and Patience. Innkeeper Renee at Gallows’ End Tavern accepted Calvin’s letter, claimed it was from her dear old mother, then told Ghoulsbie to get lost when he failed to look convinced. Apothecary Johaan took the pumpkins and sent him back toward the tavern cellar with a laced one for the Captured Scarlet Zealot. A New Plague is not a name that hides its intentions.

He learned to cook and to bind a wound in town, which is more useful than most sermons. The road paid him a little; the trainers and the town took a little more. Outside Brill, Eleanor Shackleton made him sit by her campfire until the night felt, briefly, like something a person could rest in.

He stood still in Tirisfal with Brill’s lights behind him and a list that had only changed shape. Shari Stilwell is still waiting to continue his training. Maggot Eye is still wanted. Zygand’s Scarlets are still encamped. Johaan’s pumpkin is still meant for a zealot who does not know what he is about to eat.

Deathknell is finished with him, more or less. The rest of the glades are not.

item.title: Feathers, Linen, and the Road South
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The nesting grounds southeast of Shen’dar Village smell like pride and feathers. Hippogryphs are not subtle neighbors. Teeri Wellwind had said as much: a flock had taken the rises, and travelers on the road below were learning what happens when something with an eagle’s temper decides wagon noise is an insult.
item.content:encoded:
The nesting grounds southeast of Shen’dar Village smell like pride and feathers. Hippogryphs are not subtle neighbors. Teeri Wellwind had said as much: a flock had taken the rises, and travelers on the road below were learning what happens when something with an eagle’s temper decides wagon noise is an insult.

Parzelle Starfall went anyway.

Hippogryph Youths first — loud, clumsy, all beak and bad judgment. Then the Protectors, who had already decided the highlands belonged to them. The Matriarch last, because that is how flocks keep score. Teeri wanted them thinned. Parzelle thinned them. One silver and seventy-five copper later, the High Order and the Windshapers both nodded fifty reputation’s worth of approval, which on Zephras Isle is the polite way of saying the road might be usable again by morning.

Taleen Shimmerthread wanted something quieter.

A Little Beauty is not a warrior’s errand. It is eight Hippogryph Down feathers gathered from the same nesting grounds, soft enough that Skyborne still braid them into their hair even while the island’s chains creak and the cult down in Falaath argues about who the wind really belongs to. Taleen’s point was the same as any sensible person living through a crisis: if one small thing still brings joy, you gather it. Parzelle brought the down. The feathers were silky. The Matriarch was not consulted.

Back in Shen’dar Village the Camping lessons continued under Raan Wildwind’s patient tyranny. Naleeia Tattermend — medic, cage of a captured bandit in the next room for ambiance — taught her to craft a First Aid Kit once her skill was honest enough. Injuries, Naleeia reminded her, are a reality. Offering healing at a camp might even save lives. The chronicler has heard that speech in a dozen villages. It never stops being true.

Then Tailoring.

Parzelle sat with linen and learned the apprentice shapes the island still expects of anyone who means to stay useful: Bolt of Linen Cloth, Linen Cloak, Brown Linen Shirt, Linen Bag, Simple Linen Pants. Taleen’s Camping 101: Tailoring sat newly opened in her satchel — raise the skill, earn the right to craft a Rallying Banner for a wilderness camp, remember that no camp is a camp without a fire. Camping 101: Fishing waited beside it, because even a mage who has already learned to wet a line still has to prove she can keep doing it. The High Order can argue about arcane anchors all day; someone still has to mend cloth and pull supper out of the water.

Thirty-nine minutes. A thousand copper earned, a hundred spent, which is the arithmetic of a village that sells thread cheaper than glory. No deaths today. Level eight still, which is fine — the ladder does not always move when you ask it to. She logged out on Zephras Isle with Hippogryph Harassment and A Little Beauty finished, First Aid Kit in her hands, Tailoring’s first stitches still warm, and a list that refused to shrink: Camping 101: Tailoring, Camping 101: Fishing, Restocking the Larders, Stolen Supplies, The Western Watch, Havoc in the Highlands.

The nesting grounds are quieter. The feathers are spoken for. The linen is only beginning.

The chronicler will be curious whether the next lesson she finishes is the one that teaches her to sew a banner, or the one that sends her west to a watchtower that has already learned what happens when the Faithful stop being a rumor.

item.title: The Middle Brother Finds His Range
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The plainstrider folded like laundry. Bullseye Cudsong watched it drop into the grass of Red Cloud Mesa, counted the feathers that would not stay on the bird, and did not waste the meat. In Mulgore you take what you need. The rest is a conversation with the Earth Mother that hunters are supposed to keep short.
item.content:encoded:
The plainstrider folded like laundry. Bullseye Cudsong watched it drop into the grass of Red Cloud Mesa, counted the feathers that would not stay on the bird, and did not waste the meat. In Mulgore you take what you need. The rest is a conversation with the Earth Mother that hunters are supposed to keep short.

He had been on the mesa for less time than it takes Grandmother Ohsa to finish a verse of the old grazing song. Grull Hawkwind, the chief’s son, had looked him over the way men look over a fence post they have not yet trusted with cattle, and sent him out for seven plainstrider feathers and seven pieces of meat. The camp’s stores were low. The tribe does not feed itself on promises.

Bullseye walked until the tents of Camp Narache were a smudge behind him. He keeps a pocket full of smooth round pebbles for old times’ sake, and the chronicler notes that his aim has not gotten worse since the afternoon he sat Haymaker down in the grass with one of them. The plainstriders were less impressed by family history than by the arrow that followed, which is fair of them.

Somewhere on that slope the strength of the plains settled into him, and a pillar of gold light stood up out of the grass. Level two. Another rung on a ladder that never ends, though this one smelled of feather and dust and the long open country he likes better than anything with a roof.

He carried the bundle back to Grull and was thanked in the economical Camp Narache way: you show much promise. Then the camp did what camps always do the moment a stranger proves useful. It handed him more work.

There was a hunt that continues, because hunts do, and prairie wolves do not write themselves off the list. There was a humble task from Chief Hawkwind himself, who wants someone to look in on his mother at the well southeast of camp — the kind of errand that sounds like nothing and ends with a speech. And there was a note.

The Etched Note was the one that mattered. It pointed him to Lanka Farshot, the hunter trainer of Camp Narache, who teaches the tribe how to fire a weapon that keeps the herd alive and how to know a beast before it knows you. Lanka spoke of bloodlines and elders and a road that will one day leave Mulgore for unfamiliar lands. Bullseye listened the way he watches a hawk: without blinking, without interrupting. Track Beasts settled into his hands like a language he had already been speaking under his breath.

He spent a little copper on the trades that turn a kill into a living — herbs for the bag, a knife for the hide — because a hunter who wastes nothing is only doing what his mother already taught him on the farm below Bloodhoof Village. Fourteen minutes. Forty-two copper earned, forty spent. The arithmetic of a first day that knows it is a first day.

He logged out in Mulgore with The Hunt Continues still open, the Chief’s humble task unanswered, and the open thread he has carried since before Camp Narache: a companion that walks beside him by choice. He will know it when it stares back.

The prairie wolves on the mesa have no idea what is coming. Neither, the chronicler suspects, does Bullseye — and that is the honest beginning of every hunt worth singing about.

item.title: The Wanted Poster and the Faithful
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: Vulgara’s head weighs more than a lesson. Parzelle Starfall carried it into Shen’dar Village under a sky the color of a bruise going purple, and Danarii Bellowveil took the bounty the way Peacekeepers take any good news that arrives already dead: gratefully, and without pretending the highlands are safer for it.
item.content:encoded:
Vulgara’s head weighs more than a lesson. Parzelle Starfall carried it into Shen’dar Village under a sky the color of a bruise going purple, and Danarii Bellowveil took the bounty the way Peacekeepers take any good news that arrives already dead: gratefully, and without pretending the highlands are safer for it.

Constable Aonda had posted the notice for a reason. The winged vuldren had been terrorizing the rises southwest of the village — a scourge with an appetite and a hilltop, which is all a nightmare needs on Zephras Isle. Parzelle finished what the Wanted poster asked. Six silver and a column of experience later, the High Order had one less problem and one more mage who had learned that wanted work pays in coin and in the kind of quiet that only follows something with wings being made to stop flying.

She had come back to the Shen’dar Highlands with a satchel full of yesterday’s unfinished business. A Magical Affront, aimed at Windshaper novice seers who would rather the isle keep begging spirits that have already left, came due in a wash of gold light on the cobbles of Shen’dar Village. Level seven. The chronicler has watched that light on a great many first-week mages. On a Skyborne it looks like the island agreeing, briefly, to stay up.

The rest of the day was the highlands arguing back.

Prideclaws had been pressing the village borders, bold enough that Indari Sunseam wanted pelts before someone’s child became a story instead of a warning. Parzelle brought the pelts. Bandits had been lifting windstones from Teeri Wellwind’s emergency cache and laughing about it in a cave behind a waterfall north of town — Highlands Bandits, and their leader, the one they call “Badwind” Bennic. Constable Aonda could not spare the people. Parzelle went anyway.

She died twice in the Bandit Hideout before the cave learned her name. Level seven both times. The chronicler notes these things. First deaths teach a mage whether she means it; second deaths teach her that meaning it is not the same as winning. She got up. The bandits did not, eventually. Pilfered Windstones came home. The Criminal Element closed. The waterfall kept falling, indifferent as water always is.

Then the cult.

Infiltrating the Cult was a short walk and a long idea: speak with Sania Silverstream, take the Mark of Akir, and walk into Falaath Village as if you belonged among people who have decided the Shen’dar Highlands need a different kind of faith. Missionary Jasaan met her at the entrance. Among the Faithful meant looking until the cult’s intentions stopped being rumor and started being architecture you could point at. She looked. She reported back to Aonda. The village of Shen’dar handed her the next three problems before she had finished standing up: Havoc in the Highlands, The Western Watch, Stolen Supplies.

Somewhere on a pebbly shore under the cliffs, with a Highlands Bandit cooling at her feet and the last of the pilfered stones accounted for, the strength of the isle settled into her again. Level eight. Fireball had already grown teeth. Arcane Missiles and a colder Frostbolt arrived with Polymorph, which is the mage’s polite way of saying sit still while I decide what you are for. She learned to fish, because even a Skyborne has to eat, and the island does not lower dinner from the chains.

Ninety-nine minutes across two returns to Zephras. Copper earned and spent in the ordinary arithmetic of trainers and reagents. Two deaths. A bounty finished. A cult walked into and walked back out of. Three quests still open like unfinished sentences on the highlands wind.

She logged out in Shen’dar Village with the Mark of Akir’s memory still on her and the Western Watch still waiting for someone who has already learned that Faithful is a word that means different things on different sides of the same floating island.

The chronicler will be curious which lesson she believes next: the one that says the High Order can hold the sky with spells, or the one the cult is already preaching in Falaath while the chains creak.

item.title: Under the Boughs of Aldrassil
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: Shadowglen does not hurry. The great tree Aldrassil has been listening to young night elves make their first mistakes for longer than most kingdoms have had names, and it is in no rush to be impressed.
item.content:encoded:
Shadowglen does not hurry. The great tree Aldrassil has been listening to young night elves make their first mistakes for longer than most kingdoms have had names, and it is in no rush to be impressed.

Tristan Shadowmane logged into that quiet on the morning after Forever opened, already past the first awkward hours of a druid’s life and standing at level three among the purple ferns. The Balance of Nature was open in front of him: mangy nightsabers and thistle boars grown too thick on a wet spring, the old work Conservator Ilthalaine hands every young elf who thinks the forest owes them a gentle introduction.

He killed a thistle boar. The chronicler will not dress that up. Then the strength of the wild settled into him, and a soft column of gold light rose under the boughs. Level four. Seventeen minutes. No copper earned, no copper spent, no quest turned in, and a list that still wanted six more boars and a handful of sabers before Ilthalaine would call the morning honest.

He logged out in Shadowglen with the work half-done and the tree still waiting.

The chronicler has seen longer first pages. He has rarely seen a cleaner one. The rest of Tristan’s story is still in the roots. That is for another morning.

item.title: The Light That Burns in Deathknell
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The crypt smelled of wet stone and old iron. That was the first thing Ghoulsbie noticed when the Shadow Grave spat him back into the world: not the Light, not the grave dirt under his nails, but the smell of a place that had been holding its breath for a very long time.
item.content:encoded:
The crypt smelled of wet stone and old iron. That was the first thing Ghoulsbie noticed when the Shadow Grave spat him back into the world: not the Light, not the grave dirt under his nails, but the smell of a place that had been holding its breath for a very long time.

It was the fourth of November, if the living still counted days that way. Across Azeroth the gates of Forever had opened, and for the first time the Forsaken of Tirisfal were rising with the right to call themselves paladins. The chronicler has watched a great many undead claw their way out of that same dirt. Until today, none of them had been handed a consecrated scroll and told to walk toward the pain.

Undertaker Mordo had the usual speech ready. Ghoulsbie climbed the slope into Deathknell, finished Rude Awakening, and found Shadow Priest Sarvis waiting with the two errands every newly risen corpse is given before anyone trusts them with a name: thin the Mindless Ones among the ruined graves, and take what the Damned still wear. Wolves and duskbats. Rattlecages that do not know they are already dead. Work for hands that remember a sword better than they remember a prayer.

Somewhere on that hillside the strength of something stubborn settled into him, and a pillar of gold light stood up out of the plague-grass. Level two. Then level three. The chronicler has seen that light a thousand times. On a Forsaken it looks like an argument.

Sarvis had more waiting when the bodies were counted. Marla’s Last Wish. Rattling the Rattlecages. Night Web’s Hollow. Scavenging Deathknell. The ordinary cruelty of a camp that has more dead than living and not enough of either. And then the scroll.

A Difficult Path. The consecrated parchment reeked of the Light hard enough that Sarvis asked him to step away before he opened it. Aramis Hammerhand was waiting in the little church, a paladin trainer among a people who have spent years being hunted by paladins, and his welcome was exactly as gentle as the chronicler expected: the hardest part of this new life would be rediscovering what death had taken, and enduring what it cost to take it back.

Holy Light came next. Rediscovering the Light. Heal five Injured Deathguards. The spell sat in Ghoulsbie’s hands the way a brand sits in a glove. The quest warning was honest. As a newly risen Forsaken, calling on the Light to heal would hurt. Aramis called that pain a crucible. The Deathguards outside called it other things. Some thanked him. Some told him to begone. One asked how a paladin could be standing there at all.

He did not finish the healings before the evening ended. A Light in the Darkness still waits on his list, along with the spiders and the scavenging and the wish for Marla. One hundred ninety-four copper in his pouch after the trainers took their cut. Thirty-three minutes from crypt to church door.

He logged out in Deathknell with the Light still burning under his ribs and five wounded guards still waiting for a hand that will hurt him every time he opens it.

The chronicler has known other Ghoulsbies. This one is not them. This one is a paladin, and the Light has not forgiven him yet.

item.title: Coming of Age Above the Clouds
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The wind on Zephras Isle has been wrong for centuries. The Skyborne feel it the way other people feel a missing tooth: something that used to be there, and now every breath reminds them it isn’t.
item.content:encoded:
The wind on Zephras Isle has been wrong for centuries. The Skyborne feel it the way other people feel a missing tooth: something that used to be there, and now every breath reminds them it isn’t.

Parzelle Starfall came of age on the day Forever opened, which is either excellent timing or a cosmic joke, depending on who you ask among the shen’dorei. The wind spirits that once kept their floating home aloft are gone. The anchor pylons the spirits left behind are failing. The High Order, descendants of the Highborne magisters who fled Eldre’Thalas ten thousand years ago, have decided the answer is not to wait for the spirits to return. The answer is to reclaim the arcane, walk back down to Azeroth, and learn to keep the island in the sky without begging the Elemental Plane for another favor.

Ailee Farheart sent her to Rorian the Dayseeker beneath the greatfather tree in Thendal Village. Coming of Age. A relic passed from hand to hand until the ashes are scattered to the winds. Rorian named her people plainly and set her to work: Harmony in Balance, Infestation Investigation, the small mercies and smaller cruelties of a village that can feel the magic on the wind going sour.

She died the first time in the Shen’dar Highlands before she had even finished the infestations. Level two. The chronicler notes these things. First deaths are the ones that teach a mage whether she means it. She got up.

The day unfolded the way first days do when a people are in a hurry. Elemental Unrest. Agitators among the wind sprites. Harvesting Windstones. Reading the Leylines. The Anchors of Zephras. Falling With Style, which is the High Order’s polite name for being dared off a watchtower and remembering that Walk on Air is not a metaphor. Aetheen of the Gales came to Thendal Grove to read the winds and take the measure of the newly grown. Foul Matriarch. Aggressive Encroachment. She died again in Thendal Cave, got up again, and kept the list moving.

By the time the road turned south to Shen’dar Village she was level five, and the High Order was waiting. The High Order. Welcome to Shen’dar Village. A Magical Affront aimed at Windshaper novice seers who would rather the isle stayed dependent on spirits that have already left. Cooking from Zerril Softbreeze. Level six in a column of gold light on the cobbles, with a basic campfire recipe in her hands and a staff on her back.

One hundred nine minutes. Eight hundred seventy-two copper earned, seven hundred fifteen spent, which is what happens when a mage discovers that trainers, reagents and a new life all arrive on the same invoice. Two deaths. Twenty-two quests finished. And at the end of it, a satchel full of unfinished business: Pilfered Windstones, Hippogryph Harassment, The Problem With Prideclaws, Restocking the Larders, a Wanted poster for Vulgara the Insatiable, and a Magical Affront still only partly paid.

She logged out on the Shen’dar Highlands with the island still chained to the sky and the High Order still arguing that the chains would hold if the right people learned the old spells again.

The chronicler will be curious to see which lesson she believes first: the one that says the wind will come back, or the one that says it won’t.

item.title: Wolf Meat and a Simple Rune
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: Snow in Coldridge Valley does not so much fall as it settles in and refuses to leave. The dwarves of Anvilmar have been saying that for as long as anyone can remember, which, among dwarves, is a competitive sport.
item.content:encoded:
Snow in Coldridge Valley does not so much fall as it settles in and refuses to leave. The dwarves of Anvilmar have been saying that for as long as anyone can remember, which, among dwarves, is a competitive sport.

Rip arrived in that snow on the evening Forever opened with a two-handed axe, a stubborn jaw, and the particular expression of a dwarf who has already decided the weather is personally offensive. Sten Stoutarm was waiting at the mouth of the valley the way Sten always is, with a bargain dressed up as kindness: gloves against the frostbite, if Rip would bring him eight pieces of Tough Wolf Meat from the ragged young wolves that hunt the southwestern slopes.

Rip went. The wolves were not impressed. Neither was the first Rockjaw trogg that wandered too close. Somewhere between a ragged timber wolf and a broken fang in his pack, a pillar of gold light stood up out of the snow and left him a little harder to kill. Level two. Another rung. The axe felt the same. His arms did not.

Dwarven Outfitters paid out in gloves and the next set of errands. Coldridge Valley Mail Delivery. A New Threat from Balir Frosthammer, who has opinions about Rockjaw troggs and is not shy about sharing them. And a Simple Rune, pressed into Rip’s hand while the wolf meat was still warm.

The rune pointed him into Anvilmar, to Thran Khorman, who teaches dwarves how to be warriors and complains about the cold in the same breath. Thran had the usual briefing ready: gnomes in the city because their own home blew up, dwarves taking to the Light like humans, troggs underfoot, and a promise to teach Rip how to be a real dwarf whenever he came back asking. Battle Shout settled into his throat like a habit he had not earned yet.

Twenty-six minutes. Sixty-five copper earned, ten spent. Two quests finished, two still open, and a valley full of troggs that Balir expects him to thin before anyone calls him useful.

He logged out in Anvilmar with snow in his beard and a shout he has not yet had a proper fight to use.

The mail still needs delivering. The troggs have not gone anywhere. Coldridge Valley, the chronicler notes, is very patient with beginners. It is less patient with the ones who stay beginners.

item.title: The Quiet Hunter of Red Cloud Mesa
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The plainstrider never saw him coming. This is true of most plainstriders, which is how Red Cloud Mesa keeps its reputation for being so peaceful: nothing out there lives long enough to complain.
item.content:encoded:
The plainstrider never saw him coming. This is true of most plainstriders, which is how Red Cloud Mesa keeps its reputation for being so peaceful: nothing out there lives long enough to complain.

Ruminant Cudsong had been in Camp Narache for less time than it takes a kodo to finish a mouthful. The tauren say they were once a nomadic people, roaming the Barrens and hunting the mighty kodo, and the chronicler has heard that line recited at every new calf who ever stepped into this camp. It is accurate. It is also, to a youngest son who grew up on a farm below Bloodhoof Village singing to the herd instead of hunting it, a slightly odd thing to hear in his first hour.

Grull Hawkwind, the chief’s son, had a task ready before Ruminant had finished looking around. Seven plainstrider feathers and seven pieces of meat. The camp’s stores had run low, and the old customs hold that a tauren proves himself to the Chief by feeding the tribe. A druid is not a hunter by trade. Ruminant went anyway, which is the honest definition of a first day.

He turned the question over as he walked, the way he turns every question over, and he found the plainstriders no more interested in a philosophical discussion than the chronicler would have been. They gave him their meat and their feathers, which were, strictly, not theirs to keep. Somewhere on the slope of the mesa the strength of the Earth Mother settled into him, and a pillar of gold light stood up out of the grass and left him a little taller than before. Level two. Another rung on a ladder that never ends, though this one at least came with a view.

He carried his bundle back to Grull and was thanked. The camp was pleased, in the economical way of people who say “you show promise” and consider the matter closed. And then the quest-givers of Camp Narache did what quest-givers always do the moment a stranger proves useful: they handed him more work.

There was a hunt that continues, because hunts do. There was a humble task from the Chief himself, who wants someone to look in on his mother at the well southeast of the camp, which is the sort of errand that sounds like nothing and ends with a speech. And there was a note.

The note was the one that mattered. The Verdant Note points him to Gart Mistrunner, the druid trainer of Camp Narache, who teaches tauren the Earth Mother’s old ways, the ones the night elves kept when everyone else forgot them. His mother would have cried at it. Grandmother Ohsa would have said something dry about waiting years for one of them to say something interesting.

Sixty-seven copper for the day. A new level. Three open quests and a letter he has not yet answered.

He logged out in Mulgore, seven minutes into a road that will be a great deal longer. His road runs through rougher country than his brothers’, the chronicler hears. That is for another night.

The note is still in his bag. Gart Mistrunner is still waiting.

item.title: Steel Over Sparkles: Shuffling My Azeroth Lineup
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: WoW Forever is almost here, and I’ve been doing some soul-searching. It’s the kind you do between loading screens, staring at a character select page and asking yourself who you really are. Apparently I’m someone who likes to hit things.
item.content:encoded:
WoW Forever is almost here, and I’ve been doing some soul-searching. It’s the kind you do between loading screens, staring at a character select page and asking yourself who you really are. Apparently I’m someone who likes to hit things.

For Forever, I’ve decided to go analog. That means Warrior, Rogue, Hunter and Paladin. No fireballs, no portals, and no standing in the back reading from a glowing book while someone else gets punched. The Paladin is the only one who dabbles in the Light, but he’s still a soldier first. He just brought a prayer to the sword fight. In the end, it fits my personality. Yes, I’m aware I also made the Cudsong brothers. Consistency is a virtue I’m still leveling.

Who are they, exactly? You’ll have to wait. Opening day is a name-grab free-for-all, and I’m not announcing anyone until the names are safely mine after November 4. I’ll tell you this much: I’m pretty sure they’ll all be Horde. Shocking, I know.

Retail isn’t going anywhere, but it’s changing roles. I’ll follow the same idea there, using only the classes Forever doesn’t have. That mostly leaves two: the Demon Hunter and the Death Knight. Conveniently, they’re also the two classes most likely to show up to a party looking like they lost an argument with the afterlife.

So the Retail chronicler will mostly follow two new faces:

  • Lemmindris, my Night Elf Demon Hunter (Alliance), who gave up a perfectly good soul for a set of wings and a blindfold.
  • Ghoulsbie, my Death Knight (Horde), who is technically dead and still more motivated than I am on a Monday.

Their introduction episode is coming as an extra Retail episode, this evening or tomorrow.

I’ll still play Retail, but expect a lot more Forever content than Retail for a while. Azeroth is big enough for both of me. My free time, less so.

See you in the queue on November 4.

item.description: Zul’jarra spat on the stones of Numazon and did not bother to wipe her tusks. item.content:encoded:
Zul’jarra spat on the stones of Numazon and did not bother to wipe her tusks. Behind her, the last of the Witherbark captives were limping out of the crypt into a fog so thick a man could lose his own hand in it, and in front of her lay what was left of Ritualist Zongha. She hoped, she said, that whatever loa waited for the Vilebranch in the afterlife would swallow them whole and grind them with its back teeth. Burrly did not argue. He had seen what was down there.

The mist had promised to keep, and it had. Burrly came back to Shadebasin Watch at dusk, where the pines of Zul’Aman lean over the trail like old men listening at a door, and took up the two promises he had left with. Kul’amara the Fierce had been right about the fog. It had not drifted in off any river. It had been laid down over Numazon like a blanket over a body, Vilebranch magic, so that no one on the outside would see what was being done to the Witherbark on the inside.

The Vilebranch were Malacrass’s own tribe, and Zul’jarra was not surprised that they had taken to hex magic. That was a path they chose long ago, she said, a path away from the rest of the Amani. What she would not forgive was the time. What the Vilebranch had done to the Witherbark had gone too long without an Amani answer. So the answer went in through the mist, and the mist, which had been meant to hide the Vilebranch, hid Burrly instead.

He found the crypt entrance in the grey. He cut down eight of the Vilebranch inside it, the ones who stood between him and the stairs, and then went up to where Ritualist Zongha was keeping his work. The chronicler will not describe the work. It is enough to say that Zongha is no longer doing it.

Eight Witherbark came out of the shadows alive because of him. It was only on the way out that the reason for all of it came clear, and it was worse than cruelty. The Vilebranch had not taken the Witherbark for spite. They had taken them as a gift for the Twilight’s Blade. Undead soldiers, Zul’jarra said, very quietly. Obedient soldiers. And we have already lost too many.

That is the thing about the Twilight. They never fight a war with only their own dead.

Burrly came out of Numazon heavier than he went in, in the ways that count and a few that don’t. A belt of the Spiritwarden’s make, from Amani hands, cinched around a waist that has seen too many ship’s biscuits. A Vilebranch hexxer’s mantle, taken off a man who would not need it again, though the chronicler suspects Burrly will not wear it in front of Zul’jarra. On the way through the fog he stopped, as sailors do when there is land under them and nobody shooting, to pull herbs out of the dirt and chip ore off the rocks, and from one of them he pried loose a piece of igneous stone shot through with old fire. Something the mountain coughed up. He pocketed it. The Amani paid him in coin as well, enough to jingle, which is more than the Witherbark could have offered.

Then he walked back into the mist, because the mist had not lifted.

That was the part nobody had expected. Killing the Vilebranch changed nothing. Whatever is breathing this fog over the Temple of Halazzi, it was never just them. Somewhere out there in the dark are the hash’ey shrines of the lynx, and they have to be lit before the loa will show its face. Zul’jarra held her hand up in front of her eyes, frowned at how little of it she could see, and told him not to get separated. It would try her patience, she said. She is not known for having much of it.

Burrly stood at the edge of the temple grounds with a fresh belt, a dead hexxer’s coat and a rock in his pocket, staring into a grey that stared back. The shrines are out there. So is whatever made the fog.

item.title: The Cudsong Brothers
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: Every night since the long walk out of the Barrens, somebody in the Cudsong family has sung to the kodo.
item.content:encoded:
Every night since the long walk out of the Barrens, somebody in the Cudsong family has sung to the kodo.

Not loudly, and not always well. But every night on the grass below Bloodhoof Village, when An’she has gone down behind the mesas and Mu’sha has opened her pale eye over Mulgore, a Cudsong sits on an upturned water bucket and sings low to the herd. The great beasts fold their legs, settle into the grass and chew over the day, and the song rolls over them like a blanket. The chronicler has heard it. It is the kind of music that keeps several tons of nervous animal from deciding, in the dark, that the plains wolves are closer than they are.

This is the story of three calves raised beside that song, and how they came to walk up the road to Camp Narache with a hammer, a bow and a great many questions.

The song on the trek

Before Mulgore, the tauren had no home that stayed put. They followed the herds across the Barrens, and the centaur followed them. The Kolkar raided by night and by day, and every season there were fewer tauren around the fires.

Grandmother Ohsa was already a grandmother then, a white-and-grey herd-keeper with a voice like a slow river. On the worst night of the trek, when Kolkar riders came howling out of the dark and the kodo began to bellow and pull at their tethers, she did the only thing she knew how to do. She climbed onto the lead cart and sang the old grazing songs, the ones calves learn before they learn to walk, and she kept singing while the warriors fought at the edge of the firelight. The herd did not stampede. The carts did not overturn. In the morning the warriors found the kodo lying in a great circle around Ohsa’s cart, chewing their cud as if nothing at all had happened.

The chronicler has been told by scholars that kodo do not, strictly speaking, chew cud. The scholars were not there. Neither, to be fair, was the chronicler.

“There she is,” somebody said that morning. “The cud-singer.” The family has been Cudsong ever since.

Not long after, the orcs came. Thrall’s Horde stood with Cairne Bloodhoof’s warriors against the centaur and saw the long column safely to Mulgore, where the Earth Mother’s land rises green between the mesas and the wind smells of rain. Cairne raised Thunder Bluff on the high mesa. The Cudsongs, who have never been comfortable anywhere a kodo can’t follow, settled on the plain below Bloodhoof Village. The tauren do not forget who stood beside them on their worst night. Neither do the Cudsongs. To the brothers, the Horde has never been a banner so much as a promise somebody kept.

Three calves, three colors

Tarm Cudsong, the father, is black-furred and broad, a quiet bull who carried a spear on the trek and has carried a pitchfork ever since, and much prefers the pitchfork. Sahala, the mother, is a warm tan-brown, with braids she has worn since she was a girl and a laugh you can hear from the next field. She keeps the song now, most nights, though Ohsa still takes a turn when the sky is clear.

They had three sons, and Bloodhoof Village likes to say each calf took his color from a different branch of the family, as if the Earth Mother wanted to be fair about it. The eldest rode into Mulgore as a calf in the back of a kodo cart, black as his father. The middle son was born on the trek itself, under an open sky between one camp and the next, white and grey like his grandmother. The youngest was born in Mulgore after the walking was over, tan-brown like his mother, and he is the only one of the three who has never known anything but home.

How Tohmak became Haymaker

The eldest was named Tohmak, which means something close to “stands firm” in the old herd tongue. He grew up the way a mesa does: slowly, and then all at once. By his twelfth summer he was cutting hay beside his father in the grass below Bloodhoof Village. By his fifteenth he was doing it faster than his father, and more of it, with considerably less care about where the hay ended up. “Tohmak makes hay” became a village saying for doing a great deal of work all at once and leaving someone else to tidy up after. Before long it was just Haymaker, said with a fond shake of the head.

The name got its second meaning one autumn, when a Bristleback raiding party crept up out of Brambleblade Ravine to help themselves to the winter stores. Haymaker was alone at the stacks with the big wooden mallet he used for driving fence posts. The first quilboar to reach him took one wide, honest swing to the side of the head and woke up the next morning under a haystack, with all his tusks and no memory of the afternoon. The rest of the party decided the hay was not worth it. Ever since, when anyone in Bloodhoof Village says Haymaker, they mean the swing as much as the harvest, and he lets them.

He still carries that mallet. The green bands around its head were wrapped there by his mother when the wood began to split, and he will not let anyone replace them. He wears a leather harness hung with two white tusks, which he says are trophies from that afternoon. His mother says he found them in the ravine a week later.

How Kahnu became Bullseye

The middle son was named Kahnu, after the soft rain that came the morning he was born, the first rain the column had seen in weeks. He was a quiet calf with a long, steady stare. He could watch a hawk from the moment it left the mesa until it dropped onto a field mouse half a league away, and never once blink.

His nickname came from his big brother, by way of his big brother’s forehead. When Kahnu was seven, and Tohmak was a good deal older and much too pleased about it, Tohmak spent an afternoon teasing him from the far side of the kodo pen. Kahnu said nothing. He picked up a smooth round pebble, walked off across the pasture until he was so far away that Tohmak could no longer see him, turned, and threw. The pebble came down out of the sky and struck Tohmak square between the eyes. He sat down in the grass to think about it.

Grandmother Ohsa had watched the whole thing, and laughed so hard she had to hold onto the fence. “Right in the bull’s eye,” she said, and that was that. Kahnu has been Bullseye ever since, and Haymaker, to his credit, was the first to call him by it, once his head stopped ringing.

The chronicler notes that between them, the two nicknames hold the whole Cudsong philosophy of conflict. One brother walks up and settles it. The other settles it from a long way off, before anyone knew there was a problem.

Bullseye spent the rest of his youth proving the pebble was not luck. He ran the plains with the herd scouts, learned the tracks of every plainstrider and prairie wolf between Red Cloud Mesa and the Venture Company’s noisy camps, and practiced with a short bow until the targets ran out of eyes. He wears an orange-brown vest his mother made him, and keeps a small hex-headed hammer at his belt for driving tent stakes, which he insists is a hunting tool.

Why Ruminant kept his name

Ruminant is the only brother still called by the name he was given, because he earned it before he could walk. As a calf he would sit in the grass among the resting kodo, chewing a stem of wild grass and looking at nothing at all for an hour at a time. Ohsa took one look at him and said he was ruminating, and the name came with a sense of humor already attached.

He grew into it. Ask Ruminant a question and he will answer it, eventually, after turning it over a few more times than anyone else would. He would tell you he’s just chewing things over. He braids his long brown hair and his beard with beads, the way his mother does, and wears a red and khaki robe with a fringe of claws along its edge and a blue-striped shirt beneath. He carries a small knife, which he uses for cutting herbs and, so far, for nothing else.

The hammer, the bow and the grove

So why did one become a warrior, one a hunter, and one wander so far off as to become a druid?

Haymaker’s answer is the simplest. Tarm Cudsong carried a spear on the trek because somebody had to, and he came home from the centaur wars hoping never to pick it up again. Haymaker grew up hearing the stories his father would not tell, and decided early that if anyone in the family ever had to stand between the herd and the dark again, it would be him, so that nobody else would have to. To Haymaker, a warrior is not a bull who wants a fight. He is a fence post. He goes into the ground where the trouble will come, and he does not move. That he enjoys the swinging part is, he admits, a happy accident.

Bullseye’s answer is the land. The tauren are hunters as much as herders, and the old hunt in Mulgore is a kind of prayer: take only what you need, thank the Earth Mother for it, waste nothing. Bullseye loves the open plains more than anything with a roof, likes animals better than most people, and has always preferred to solve a problem before it gets close enough to breathe on him. He means to find a companion out there, some beast that will walk beside him by choice. He says he will know it when it stares back.

Ruminant’s answer is the long one. For as long as anyone could remember, the tauren had kept the Earth Mother’s ways through their shamans and the old rites. The path of the druid had been lost to them for generations. Then Hamuul Runetotem went far to the north and learned it again from the night elves, of all people, and from the demigod Cenarius himself. He came home to Thunder Bluff an Arch Druid and opened his teaching on Elder Rise. Some elders were glad. Others, and the Grimtotem loudest among them, grumbled that a tauren had no business learning the Earth Mother’s ways from elves who stand with the Alliance.

Ruminant heard the grumbling, chewed it over for most of a year, and then rode the long lift up to Elder Rise to listen to Hamuul for himself. What he heard there was not an elven idea or a tauren one. It was that the land belongs to no side. That tauren and night elves of the Cenarion Circle sit together in Moonglade under the same moon and tend the same world, and that a druid’s work is to help keep it whole. Ruminant came home and told his family he meant to walk farther from home than any Cudsong since the trek, and that one day the road would take him all the way to Moonglade.

His mother cried a little. His grandmother said she had been waiting years for one of them to say something interesting. His father said nothing for a long while, and then asked whether druids still had to help with the milking. They do. Ruminant went anyway.

The chronicler suspects the family is prouder of this than it lets on. The Cudsongs have always been the ones who keep the herd together on a bad night. Ruminant simply decided the herd was bigger than he had been told.

The road to Camp Narache

They set out together before dawn, on the road up to Red Cloud Mesa, where Chief Hawkwind keeps Camp Narache and young tauren go to be tested before the world is allowed to have them. They took almost nothing. Haymaker had his mallet and his harness. Bullseye had his vest, his little hammer and a pocket full of smooth round pebbles, for old times’ sake. Ruminant had his knife, his braids and a great many unanswered questions. Their roads will not always run side by side, and Ruminant’s, the chronicler hears, runs through rougher country than his brothers’. That is a worry for another day.

Their mother sang them as far as the edge of the pasture. The kodo, who have never once been told anything, stood up and watched them go.

Three brothers. A warrior who goes where the trouble is, a hunter who meets it a long way out, and a druid who would like to understand it before anybody has to swing at anything. The chronicler has seen worse families set out with better gear, and most of them did not get far. These three have the song.

The plainstriders on the mesa have no idea what is coming. Neither do the Bristleback. Neither, the chronicler suspects, do the brothers.

item.title: The Sunwalker at Fairbreeze
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The tauren say An’she was wounded by the shadows long ago, and that the sun still bleeds a little every morning to warn the world that dawn is coming. The Sunwalkers greet that wound with drums. They gather in the dark before first light, beat out the yeena’e, and call on the ancestors who died saving lives to help the sun climb.
item.content:encoded:
The tauren say An’she was wounded by the shadows long ago, and that the sun still bleeds a little every morning to warn the world that dawn is coming. The Sunwalkers greet that wound with drums. They gather in the dark before first light, beat out the yeena’e, and call on the ancestors who died saving lives to help the sun climb.

Somebody has to feed them afterward.

For years that somebody was a broad young tauren who kept the smoke pit behind the Sunwalker camp, rising long before the drummers to bank the coals so that when An’she cleared the horizon there would be meat ready for the faithful. The Sunwalkers, who are a pious order and not a subtle one, started calling the pit-keeper Dawnbrisket. The name stuck the way smoke sticks to fur. You can wash it all you like.

The pit-keeper listened while the meat turned. Listened to Chieftain Aponi Brightmane say that the dawn will come, that the balance will shift back to where it should be. Listened to the old ones argue whether the sun’s light and the Light of the priests were the same thing. And somewhere in all that listening, An’she answered. The first time the Light came, it came as warmth in his hands, which for a cook is a very confusing way to be chosen.

Then the Void came for the Sunwell. The elves’ great fount in Quel’Thalas was torn open into a swirling wound in the sky, and Aponi took her Sunwalkers north to pour An’she’s light into it while the siege raged. Dawnbrisket was left behind to mind the camp. Someone has to. The chronicler has met a great many heroes who were left behind to mind the camp. They tend to arrive later with something to prove.

By the time Dawnbrisket reached the war, the siege was a story people told in inns. Ula’tek had fallen. Quel’Thalas and Zul’Aman were trying out a peace neither of them trusted, and beneath the Coiled Isle something older than both was waking. A cook-turned-paladin, it turns out, is right on time for the second half of anything.

The road began, as roads do now, in Dornogal. Letters waited there with the seals of The Weaver, The Vizier and The General, people in Khaz Algar who expect to be noticed. A purse found its way into the Sunwalker’s hands as well, heavy enough to make a camp cook sit down for a moment. Dawnbrisket took the letters, took the purse, and went to Silvermoon City.

The elves cry “by the light of the sun” when they go to war. The chronicler watched a Sunwalker step into the Sanctum of Light and wondered whether anyone there had ever considered that the sun might have other friends.

Silvermoon put the newcomer to work at once. Magister Astalor Bloodsworn, who believes the city’s safety lies in methods his colleagues would rather not hear about, was waiting near the harbor with what he called a guest. The guest was a gnarldin in a cage, and it made its position on being called prey very clear. Astalor walked Dawnbrisket through his instruments: a crystal vessel, two traps, and the anguish the hunted leave behind, which the magister means to distill into wards for the city. The chronicler has heard worse ideas from elves, but not many.

Then Astalor opened the cage to make a point. The gnarldin made one back. Dawnbrisket survived the ambush, which is the only kind of graduation Astalor offers, and went back to the magister’s sanctum with a hunter’s license and a first name on the list: Magister Sunbreaker. A magister of Silvermoon with “Sunbreaker” for a name, now hunted by a servant of the sun. Somebody up there has a sense of humor.

In between, there were smaller rites. A handful of Hallow’s End sweets from the candy bucket at the inn, the elves applauding as though a war had been won. A wander through the Bazaar. And lessons in the pick and the sickle, because a Sunwalker who can pull ore from rock and herbs from the ground will never be a burden to the people he serves. Dawnbrisket paid the trainers what they asked and did not haggle. That is the cook in him. You always pay the person who feeds you.

Then the Path of Dawn, gold under the leaves, and Fairbreeze Village. Magistrix Landra Dawnstrider had three troubles waiting. Wild beasts were crowding into the village, driven from the woods. Strange Lightbloom was sprouting where it had no business growing. And a lynx the villagers call Sharpmaw had begun eyeing their children. Dawnbrisket took all three in hand.

And then the village turned out to have a fourth trouble, one the magistrix had not mentioned.

Two Alliance strangers were working Fairbreeze that evening, a hunter with arcane arrows and a rogue who struck out of the shadows with blades and black powder. The first time they caught the Sunwalker it was a surprise. The second time, it was an argument. By the third and fourth, it was a lesson. Four times Dawnbrisket fell among the pretty white houses of Fairbreeze, and four times An’she, who knows something about wounds that do not close, let the Sunwalker rise.

After the fourth, Dawnbrisket left the field. The chronicler does not count that as a defeat. The chronicler counts it as a cook who knows when the meat is ruined and the fire needs to be built again.

Sharpmaw still prowls. The Lightbloom keeps creeping toward the houses. Magister Sunbreaker’s name is still on Astalor’s list, and the Vilebranch are still stalking the woods. And somewhere in Eversong, a hunter and a rogue are telling each other about the big tauren in Fairbreeze.

They should enjoy it. The sun rises every morning.

item.title: The Eagle on Akil’zon’s Reach
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The ledge at the top of the Temple of Akil’zon has no railing, and the wind up there has no manners. Zul’jarra stood at its edge with her eyes closed, trying to remember a lesson from her childhood. The eagle loa, her uncle used to say, is the loa of victory, but also of oaths and conviction. item.content:encoded:
The ledge at the top of the Temple of Akil’zon has no railing, and the wind up there has no manners. Zul’jarra stood at its edge with her eyes closed, trying to remember a lesson from her childhood. The eagle loa, her uncle used to say, is the loa of victory, but also of oaths and conviction. Then the trial came clear, and it was the simplest one in the world. Jump.

Burrly jumped. The chronicler will not pretend to know what a Kul Tiran thinks on the way down. Whatever he thought, the mountain did not have him.

The evening had begun in a city that was already lost. Burrly came back to the Altar of Malacrass, where the frightened of Atal’Aman had been told to gather, and spent the dusk running errands for a people who had spent centuries killing men who looked like him. He went looking for the missing elders, and among them found old Kinduru, the loa speaker, who would not leave until he had the Hash’ey Staff in hand. He proved his worth to Amani who did not want to be impressed. He took up arms blessed by the Light, which in a troll city is its own kind of joke. At Ragemaw Terrace he beat out the fires the Twilight’s Blade had set in the last of the Amani lightwood, because without that wood there would be no ballista and without the ballista there would be no shot at Mor’duun.

He cut down the Twilight Ritualists at Firewing Terrace, the ones dragging fresh cultists into the city through their dark circles, and the Trollbreakers who had already come through. He bled the Twilight where he found it. Then Zul’jan’s ballista was ready, and Burrly manned it while Zul’jarra and Lady Liadrin went to distract the general. He broke the shadows that warded Mor’duun and brought down the general’s barrier.

It did not save the city. Zul’jarra had said as much before the first bolt flew. There was too much Void in the stones, too much ruin. Atal’Aman was truly lost, and the best a ballista could buy was time for the people to run.

So they ran, to Amani’Zar Village, where Zul’jarra warned him that her people kill strangers on sight and that she could only run so fast if one of them thought he had looked at them wrong. He kept his weapons where they could be seen. He cooked for refugees beside Torundo, her war advisor, which is not a sentence the chronicler expected to write about a sailor. And there, among the tired and the displaced, Kinduru said something no one wanted to hear. The old way. The path of the hash’ey. Zul’jarra called it a tale for children. Then, because she had run out of other tales, she agreed to try it.

Akil’zon’s Reach sits at the foot of the mountains, and the gnarldin had moved in. Big, nomadic, keeping to themselves until recently, and lately breaking the old shrines and eating the eagles. Burrly broke a dozen of them. Zul’jarra, who said she did not know Akil’zon but did know giants, asked for the heads of their three fiercest warriors, Brulagh the Crusher, Cragward Gaahl and Pulverizer Helthra. Burrly brought her all three. She took one by the hair and admired it the way other women admire jewelry. He kept Brulagh’s torque for his own neck, which is the sort of souvenir that tells you how far a man has come from Boralus.

He lit the four Hash’ey Shrines up the mountainside, and the last one at the top. He carried the heads to the temple as an offering, and the eagles, for the first time in years, came back to watch.

And somewhere in the gnarldin country the world coughed up something strange, a little carved thing of the forest that is said to call down green spirit birds out of nowhere to fall on its bearer’s enemies. On Akil’zon’s own mountain. The chronicler does not believe in signs. The chronicler wrote it down anyway.

After the jump, the eagle answered. Zul’jarra felt the blessing buffet her like a gale, and with it came the truth she had been dreading. The loa had been there all along. It was her grandfather, Zul’jin, who broke the bond. It was up to her to mend it.

Burrly stood on the temple stones afterward and felt it again, the thickening of arm and back that comes from surviving one more thing that meant to kill him. Another rung. The mountain did not notice.

Akil’zon pointed them on to Halazzi, the loa of the Witherbark, and at Shadebasin Watch Kul’amara the Fierce told them how the road there runs. But first there is the mist, and Numazon Crypt inside it, where the Vilebranch have been doing to the Witherbark what the Twilight did to Atal’Aman. Zul’jarra means to take a life for every life they took. Burrly carries two promises out of the watch: one to cut through the crypt, the other to bring back whoever the shadows have not yet finished with.

He has not started on either. The mist will keep.

item.title: The Traitors of Tranquillien
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The pamphlets were the first thing to burn. They always are. Laotou walked into Tranquillien at dusk to find the Twilight’s Blade nailing its gospel to every post and doorframe in town, and the monk, who has never once been persuaded by a pamphlet, set about tearing them down.
item.content:encoded:
The pamphlets were the first thing to burn. They always are. Laotou walked into Tranquillien at dusk to find the Twilight’s Blade nailing its gospel to every post and doorframe in town, and the monk, who has never once been persuaded by a pamphlet, set about tearing them down.

The cult had been living here a long while, it turned out. Their cover was blown now, so they had stopped pretending and started fighting in the open, which is the only honest thing a cult ever does. Voidlings crawled out from between the houses. Obelisks hummed in the square. There were supply crates to smash and effigies to break, and Laotou broke them, one after another, with the patient rhythm of someone sweeping a floor.

Arator stood among the wreckage and would not let the town fall. The governor had made his terms plain: join the Blade or be executed. So while the fighting went on, the Pandaren went door to door pulling frightened elves out of the line of fire. Healers are good at this part. Nobody writes songs about it, but nobody who was carried out of a burning house forgets who did the carrying.

Then came the ugly work. The traitors of Tranquillien were not strangers. Ranger Lethvalin. Matron Narsilla. Guard Captain Leonic. Names the town had trusted for years, the sort of people who teach the young ones their trade and keep the watch at night. All three wore the Blade’s colors under their cloaks. The chronicler has seen this before, in Lordaeron, in Stormwind, in every city that thought itself too proud to rot. The rot never comes from outside. Laotou cut them down, and Tranquillien was quieter afterward, though not in any way that felt like peace.

From the traitors’ leavings the monk took up a Twilight Agitator’s Stave, held it for the space of a breath, and set it down again in favor of the old Mistdancer Staff. The chronicler approves. A healer should not carry a weapon that was made to stir up crowds.

Magister Umbric had gone missing in the confusion, off chasing Antenorian, the governor who had sold the town. Umbric had his reasons. Kasiea was dead, her research torn from her body, and grief makes a man careless about what waits around corners. Laotou found the trail through a secretary named Faloria, who had a jeweled key and a strongbox and a great deal to answer for. Inside the box were plans of infiltration and a stack of spare pamphlets. Cults are nothing if not well stocked.

Umbric was alive. Angry, but alive.

The cult had marked other places on its maps, and one of them was Windrunner Village, the old seat of the family whose name still makes rangers stand a little straighter. So the road went on, past the Hollow Grove, to a village too quiet for anyone’s comfort. Laotou went about waking the old ranger constructs that slump at its borders, arcane golems gone to rust and moss, and set them back on their feet to stand guard and sniff out snakes in the grass. The monk came away from it with a pair of tights once tailored for a Twilight spy. Spoils are spoils. The chronicler does not ask.

Upstairs in the village, Umbric tried one last ritual. Arator talked. Laotou carried four void shards out of the balconies and fed them, one by one, into the dark sphere at the center of the room, and watched it swell with each. Whatever Umbric learned there, he did not like it. The monk wore a depleted voidshard ring away from that room and gathered a mote of light on the way out, as if the world were trying to even the scales.

Then south, to the Ruins of Deatholme, where Dar’Khan Drathir once kept house for the Scourge and where nothing good has grown since. The Twilight’s Blade has chosen it for a fortress. Fitting, Umbric said. Valeera Sanguinar was waiting there, quiet as a knife in a sleeve. She had tracked Antenorian to a cavern beneath the ruins.

He has gone in. Laotou has not, yet. The cavern waits, and so does the governor, and so do the missing pages of a dead woman’s notes.

item.title: What Are People Rolling in WoW Forever? X vs Bluesky
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: WoW Forever launches on November 4, 2026, and name reservation opens just before that. Like a lot of you, I’ve spent the beta weeks reading everyone’s “here’s my main” posts and wondering which way the crowd is going. Horde or Alliance? PvP or RP? How many Undead Paladins is Azeroth about to get?
item.content:encoded:
WoW Forever launches on November 4, 2026, and name reservation opens just before that. Like a lot of you, I’ve spent the beta weeks reading everyone’s “here’s my main” posts and wondering which way the crowd is going. Horde or Alliance? PvP or RP? How many Undead Paladins is Azeroth about to get?

So I went and counted. I read through public posts on X and Bluesky from the start of the beta to now and tallied what people said they’re planning to play. I kept the two networks separate, because it turns out they really don’t agree.

How I collected the data

  • Date range: September 17, 2026 (beta launch day) through October 25, 2026.
  • Where: X, using search of public posts, and Bluesky, using its public search. I didn’t sign in to either one.
  • What counted: only clear statements about the person’s own choice, like “I’m maining a Tauren Druid.” Questions, jokes, ads, bots, news, guides and “still deciding” posts were skipped.
  • One vote per person: each person counts once, by their stated main. Alts are ignored. If someone only mentioned a character they played in the beta and never stated a plan, I counted that, but treated it as weaker evidence.
  • How much:
    • X: about 35 searches turned up 562 posts. I read 483 of them closely and counted 226 people.
    • Bluesky: I scanned 6,037 posts, read 239 that talked about picks, and counted 105 people.

Known gaps

  • The X giveaway thread. One X giveaway asked people to comment the class they’re playing. That gave me 41 class-only replies, but they came with a prize attached. I show the X class numbers with and without them.
  • Partial reply threads on X. X search only returns part of big reply threads. The giveaway had 864 replies, and search found about 44 of them.
  • Bluesky paging. Bluesky’s public search wouldn’t go past the first page of results. I searched in two-day windows and took the first page of each, so some posts were missed.
  • Not a random sample. These are English posts from people who chose to share their pick. Very few people named a ruleset or a spec, so treat those numbers as hints.
